DeFT-RAG: Incrementally Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers

CCS: Information systems Question answeringCCS: Computing methodologies Natural language generation
Dingyi Kang Affiliation: University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas, USA email: dingyi.kang@utdallas.edu and Bingzhe Li Affiliation: University of Texas at Dallas, Richardson, Texas, USA email: bingzhe.li@utdallas.edu
Abstract.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

Keywords: 
Retrieval-augmented generation, multi-hop question answering, question decomposition

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) now perform strongly across a wide range of language tasks (OpenAI, 2023; Yang et al., 2025). Yet because their knowledge is stored in their parameters, they often answer incorrectly when that knowledge is outdated or missing, and they may hallucinate (Huang et al., 2025). Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Lewis et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2023) mitigates this by retrieving passages from an external corpus and grounding the answer in them, which improves accuracy on knowledge-intensive tasks without retraining the model.

A single retrieve-then-generate step suffices when one passage holds the answer, but it falls short on multi-hop question answering (Yang et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2022), where answering one question requires chaining several facts spread across different documents: retrieving with the question alone returns passages that match its surface terms, and these rarely cover every link of the chain. Graph-based RAG methods (Edge et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026) address this by building a graph over the corpus that links entities and passages, then retrieving passages by following links from the entities in the question. However, a multi-hop chain runs through bridge entities that the question never names and that only become known once an earlier step is answered. Because most graph-based methods retrieve once per question, starting from the entities the question names, they can reach the bridge entities only by following graph links from those entities, which rarely gets past the first one: for most of these methods, the full evidence chain is retrieved for only 6–10% of 3-hop MuSiQue questions (Figure 1a, Table 3).

Iterative RAG methods (Trivedi et al., 2023; Press et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2026b; Kim et al., 2026) instead aim to find these bridge entities directly: they decompose the question into sub-questions and alternate between retrieval and LLM reasoning, so each answered sub-question supplies the bridge entity needed by the next retrieval. However, their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, often within one call, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding the dependencies among them, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known, each of which leads to its own type of error. Specifically, a plan written before any sub-question is answered must guess bridge entities, and a wrong guess or a missing step misleads every later step (planning errors). The dependencies decided among the sub-questions may link them wrongly or in the wrong order, so a sub-question is searched before the fact it needs is found (dependency errors), as in Figure 1b. When an answer arrives, the LLM may fail to rewrite the sub-question that depends on it, which keeps a placeholder instead of the entity’s name, or may rewrite it with the wrong entity (rewriting errors). In a long, growing input, the LLM may also lose track of what it has already found (tracking errors), as in Figure 1c. Moreover, fixed top-kk retrieval, used by most RAG methods, makes these issues worse by lowering the answer accuracy at each step. Finally, iterative methods discard their intermediate results once a question is answered, although multi-hop questions over the same corpus often share intermediate facts that could be reused.

Based on these observations, we propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs), until these accumulated QA pairs are enough to answer the original question. Each sub-question names every entity it asks about and does not depend on the answer to any other sub-question. Since nothing is planned in advance, no bridge entity has to be guessed before it is found, and there are no dependencies to get wrong and no sub-question to rewrite. This avoids planning, dependency and rewriting errors, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time: writing a sub-question for the next missing piece of information. Second, DeFT-RAG converts the remaining LLM work into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM. A QA table keeps every QA pair and is updated by rules, without any model call, so the LLM no longer has to keep track of what is known, which avoids tracking errors. A fine-tuned lightweight decision model (DM), a language model trained to answer yes/no questions with a probability (StartLux Labs, 2026), makes a few yes/no decisions: whether a question can be answered directly, whether the QA pairs found so far are enough, and whether retrieved passages are relevant, so that the LLM sees more of the needed passages and fewer distracting ones. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning, which saves retrieval and LLM calls. Together, these designs raise the accuracy of each step and of the final answer, while making the intermediate answers reusable across questions. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose an incremental question decomposition that generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the QA pairs found so far. It removes the need to plan sub-questions, decide their dependencies or rewrite them, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task: writing the sub-question for the next missing piece of information.

  • •

    We convert the remaining LLM work into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table, and yes/no decisions by a fine-tuned lightweight DM, such as whether retrieved passages are relevant. This aims to raise the accuracy of each step, and to leave the LLM only a few focused, fine-grained tasks that require text generation.

  • •

    We design a QA cache that reuses the answers to earlier sub-questions for later questions that ask a sub-question with the same meaning, which saves retrieval and LLM calls.

  • •

    We evaluate DeFT-RAG on three multi-hop QA benchmarks with two LLM backbones. It achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method, and reusing answers through the QA cache further reduces LLM calls without lowering accuracy. To support reproducibility, we release our code and prompts at https://github.com/Dingyi-Kang/DeFT-RAG.

2. Background and Problem Formulation

This section introduces RAG and multi-hop question answering, and the limitations of existing methods on such questions; Section 5 discusses related work in more detail.

2.1. Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Given a corpus 𝒞\mathcal{C} of passages and a question QQ, a vanilla RAG system answers

(1) a=LLM⁡(Q,R⁡(Q,𝒞)),a=\mathrm{LLM}\big(Q,\,R(Q,\mathcal{C})\big),

where RR retrieves the passages relevant to QQ from 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Vanilla RAG implements RR as similarity search, whether by dense-embedding cosine or sparse lexical matching (BM25), ranking passages by their similarity to the query:

(2) Rk​(q,𝒞)=top​-​kp∈𝒞⁡s​(e⁡(q),e⁡(p)),R_{k}(q,\mathcal{C})=\operatorname*{top\text{-}k}_{p\in\mathcal{C}}\;s\big(e(q),\,e(p)\big),

where e⁡(⋅)e(\cdot) maps a query or passage to its representation and ss is a similarity function. We refer to Eq. (2) as fixed top-kk similarity retrieval: the number of passages kk is fixed in advance, and passages are ranked only by their similarity to the query.

2.2. Multi-Hop Question Answering

A multi-hop question usually cannot be answered from a single passage (Yang et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2020; Trivedi et al., 2022). Answering it requires an evidence chain of two or more facts, each stated in a passage of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, where some facts can only be found once an earlier one is known. We call the intermediate answers that later facts depend on bridge entities: the chain passes through them, but QQ never names them. For example, to answer “Where do greyhound buses leave from in the city where the performer of Darlings formed?”, one must first find that Darlings is an album by Kevin Drew, then that he formed his band, Broken Social Scene, in Toronto, and only then where Greyhound buses leave from there (the Toronto Coach Terminal). Kevin Drew and Toronto are the bridge entities (top of Figure 1).

Vanilla RAG (Eq. (1)) handles such questions poorly. Eq. (2) ranks passages only by their similarity to QQ, so for the Darlings question it returns passages that share its words, such as passages about greyhound dogs, a Greyhound coach model and a person named Darling. Answering QQ, however, also needs passages about Kevin Drew and Toronto. Because QQ never mentions either of them, their passages rank low, and a single retrieval rarely returns the full evidence chain: on MuSiQue, vanilla RAG retrieves it for only 7% of 3-hop questions (Table 3). To address this, two lines of work have been developed: graph-based RAG (§2.3) and iterative RAG (§2.4).

2.3. Graph-Based RAG

Graph-based RAG methods build a graph over 𝒞\mathcal{C} offline, either by using an LLM to extract the entities in every passage and the relations between them (Edge et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2024), or by linking passages across documents through the entities they share (Zhuang et al., 2026). At answering time, they locate the entities mentioned in QQ in this graph and follow its links to collect related passages, instead of ranking passages only by their similarity to QQ as in Eq. (2). In this way, evidence linked to the question’s entities can be retrieved even when it shares little wording with QQ.

However, graph-based RAG still falls short in covering the full evidence chain once a question needs more than two hops: on MuSiQue, most graph-based methods retrieve the full chain for only 6–10% of 3-hop questions, barely above vanilla RAG (Table 3); LinearRAG reaches 28%, but only by giving the LLM about 4,100 words of passages per question, nearly five times as many as vanilla RAG, most of which are not part of the evidence chain. The reason is that most graph-based methods retrieve only once per question, starting from the entities QQ names, while the bridge entities are by definition not mentioned in QQ, so the retrieval can reach them only by following graph links from those entities, which rarely gets past the first bridge entity. In Figure 1a, HippoRAG 2 learns from the album passage that Darlings is by Kevin Drew, but retrieves no passage about his band or Toronto, and answers from a passage about Greyhound in Philadelphia.

2.4. Iterative RAG

Iterative RAG methods instead aim to find these bridge entities directly: rather than preprocessing the corpus, they decompose QQ into sub-questions and alternate between retrieval and LLM reasoning, so that each sub-question can name the bridge entity found in an earlier step and reach passages that a search with QQ alone would miss. As shown in Table 3, iterative methods retrieve the full evidence chain for 19–41% of 3-hop questions, well above most graph-based methods.

However, iterative methods often fail, because they ask the LLM to perform several tasks, often within one call: planning sub-questions before any of them is answered, deciding the dependency links among them, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. Each of these tasks leads to its own type of error. First, planning errors: methods that plan the sub-questions in advance, such as LogicRAG (Chen et al., 2026b) and REAP (Zhu et al., 2026), must guess bridge entities before finding them, and a wrong guess or a missing step misleads every later step. For example, asked “Who is the owner of the record label of the guitarist who performed on the Top Gun theme?”, LogicRAG’s plan asks for the label of the theme’s composer instead of first finding the guitarist, so it answers with the owner of the wrong label. Second, dependency errors: methods that link the sub-questions by their dependencies, such as LogicRAG and REAP, may link them wrongly or in the wrong order, so a sub-question is searched before the fact it depends on is found. In Figure 1b, LogicRAG searches for the city where “the performer” formed before it has found the performer, retrieves passages about bands from other cities, and never searches for the performer at all.

Third, rewriting errors: when the answer to a sub-question arrives, methods such as Hi-Q (Kim et al., 2026) and REAP must rewrite the sub-question that depends on it. The LLM may fail to do so, and the sub-question keeps a placeholder instead of the entity’s name, so retrieval often cannot find the passages about this bridge entity; or it may rewrite the sub-question with the wrong entity. Fourth, tracking errors: methods that carry their whole reasoning history in the prompt, such as IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023) and Self-Ask (Press et al., 2023), must find what is already known within a long and growing input, and may miss a fact they have already found or ask for it again. In Figure 1c, IRCoT’s input holds all three gold passages, and its reasoning states that the band is based in Toronto, yet it then follows a passage about Greyhound in Philadelphia and answers with the Philadelphia terminal.

Moreover, fixed top-kk retrieval (Eq. (2)), used by most RAG methods, makes these issues worse, because it lowers the answer accuracy of every step. With a small kk, part of the needed evidence is missed; with a large kk, the evidence is buried among distracting passages. Table 1 illustrates this on MuSiQue questions that can be answered in one retrieval step: widening the list from the top 5 to the top 10 passages raises how often all needed passages are present from 62% to 88%, yet accuracy barely changes (0.620 to 0.630); keeping only the gold passages from the top 10 raises it to 0.793. 2Wiki shows the same pattern. Since iterative methods answer several sub-questions in sequence, and each step depends on the answers before it, these errors add up across steps and greatly increase the chance that the whole process fails.

Finally, compared with vanilla RAG and graph-based RAG, iterative methods spend many more retrieval and LLM calls to answer a question (Appendix E), which are expensive in latency and cost, yet once a question is answered, they discard the intermediate sub-questions and answers. This is wasteful: multi-hop questions over the same corpus often share intermediate facts, so these answers could be reused to save retrieval and LLM calls for later questions.

3. DeFT-RAG Design

DeFT-RAG is built on three components (Figure 2): incremental question decomposition (§3.1); fine-grained tasks outside the LLM, namely rule-based updates to a QA table (§3.2) and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model (DM) (§3.3); and reusing answers across questions through a QA cache (§3.4). §3.5 shows how they work together to answer a question. We call a task fine-grained when it does only one thing at a time, from a short input, such as making one yes/no decision, or generating a new sub-question without the need to rewrite the others.

3.1. Incremental Question Decomposition

In DeFT-RAG, the LLM performs only three fine-grained tasks:

(3) qt+1=LLMsub​(Q,Ft),a=LLMans​(q,P),a^=LLMfin​(Q,F)q_{t+1}=\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}}(Q,F_{t}),\;\;a=\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{ans}}(q,P),\;\;\hat{a}=\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{fin}}(Q,F)

where Ft={(q1,a1),…,(qt,at)}F_{t}=\{(q_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(q_{t},a_{t})\} is the QA table, the set of QA pairs (sub-questions with their answers) found after tt steps, and PP is the set of passages selected for a question (§3.3). LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} writes the next sub-question, LLMans\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{ans}} answers a question from its selected passages, and LLMfin\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{fin}} answers the original question from the QA table (blue in Figure 2).

LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the QA pairs found so far, asking for the next missing piece of information, until the DM judges these QA pairs enough to answer the original question (§3.3). A sub-question is self-contained when it names every entity it asks about, by name or by a description that needs no other lookup, and does not depend on the answer to any other sub-question, so it can be searched and answered on its own. For example, once the QA table shows that the Rhine ends in the North Sea, “Where does the North Sea meet the Atlantic?” is self-contained, while “Where does that sea meet the Atlantic?” is not, because “that sea” points to an earlier step. Since nothing is planned in advance, no bridge entity has to be guessed before it is found, which avoids the planning errors of §2.4. Since no sub-question depends on another, there are no dependencies to get wrong and no sub-question to rewrite, which avoids dependency and rewriting errors. More importantly, the LLM can focus on a single fine-grained task at a time: writing a sub-question for the next missing piece of information. Together, these improve the quality of the question decomposition and help DeFT-RAG find every bridge entity of the evidence chain: it retrieves the full chain for more questions with three or more hops than any other system in Table 3.

3.2. QA Table

DeFT-RAG converts the rest of the work that iterative methods leave to the LLM into fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table, described here, and yes/no decisions made by the DM (§3.3). This aims to raise the accuracy of each step, and to leave the LLM only the three tasks in Eq. 3, which require text generation.

Instead of tracking everything found so far within the LLM’s context, in a long and growing prompt of passages and past reasoning, DeFT-RAG keeps it in a compact form, the QA table FtF_{t} of Eq. 3, which starts empty, F0=∅F_{0}=\emptyset, and grows by one QA pair at each step that finds an answer:

(4) Ft+1=Ft∪{(qt+1,at+1)}.F_{t+1}=F_{t}\cup\{(q_{t+1},a_{t+1})\}.

The QA table is updated by rules, without any LLM or DM call: the QA pair of each answered sub-question is added to the table; a sub-question that gets no answer is recorded, and LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} is shown it so that it is not asked again; and a new sub-question that repeats one already asked is detected by comparing the normalized wording, and LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} is asked for another one. Figure 2 shows the QA table for an example question. Every answer found is thus kept explicitly as a QA pair, rather than buried in a long prompt, which avoids tracking errors. The QA table is the only record of what is known passed from one step to the next: LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} reads it to write the next sub-question, the DM reads it to decide whether enough is known to stop, and LLMfin\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{fin}} reads it to answer the original question. Since each QA pair is a self-contained sub-question with a short answer, these inputs stay short and name every entity found so far, instead of carrying long passages or the wording of earlier steps.

3.3. Decision Tasks

The DM is a language model, usually with far fewer parameters than the backbone LLM, trained to answer yes/no questions with a probability (StartLux Labs, 2026) and fine-tuned for our decisions (§4.2). DeFT-RAG makes three types of yes/no decisions with it (orange in Figure 2), which the LLM would otherwise have to make:

  • •

    Relevance: Drel​(q,p)D_{\mathrm{rel}}(q,p) decides whether a retrieved passage pp is relevant to a question qq.

  • •

    Direct answer: Ddirect​(Q,Rw​(Q,𝒞))D_{\mathrm{direct}}(Q,R_{w}(Q,\mathcal{C})) decides whether the top ww passages retrieved for the original question, Rw​(Q,𝒞)R_{w}(Q,\mathcal{C}), already contain all the evidence needed, so that QQ can be answered in one step.

  • •

    Enough facts: Dsuff​(Q,Ft)D_{\mathrm{suff}}(Q,F_{t}) decides whether the QA pairs found so far are enough to answer QQ, which ends the loop.

For each decision, the DM reads a short input xx, such as a question and a passage, and returns the probability that the answer is yes. The decision is

(5) D(x)=𝟙[pDM(yes∣x)≥τ],D(x)=\mathbb{1}\big[\,p_{\mathrm{DM}}(\text{yes}\mid x)\geq\tau\,\big],

with a fixed threshold τ\tau for each type. Since the DM’s probability of yes reflects how often yes is actually right (Appendix C), we use τ=0.5\tau=0.5, “more likely yes than no”, for relevance and enough facts, and a stricter τ=0.7\tau=0.7 for direct answer, because a question that needs several steps but is wrongly answered directly is unlikely to get the right answer, while a question that one step could answer but is wrongly sent to the loop can still get the right answer there, only with more LLM calls.

Passage selection.

For relevance, the DM keeps, from the top ww passages retrieved for qq, those relevant to qq:

(6) Select⁡(q,Rw​(q,𝒞))={p∈Rw​(q,𝒞):Drel​(q,p)=1}.\mathrm{Select}\big(q,R_{w}(q,\mathcal{C})\big)=\{\,p\in R_{w}(q,\mathcal{C}):D_{\mathrm{rel}}(q,p)=1\,\}.

Because only the selected passages reach the LLM, ww can be larger than the kk of the usual top-kk retrieval (Eq. (2)) without burying the evidence among distracting passages (§2.4). All settings are listed in Table 6.

Fine-tuning.

We fine-tune the DM with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), using labels derived only from the gold annotations of each benchmark’s training split, such as which passages hold the evidence for a question and which intermediate answers it needs. No test question is used. Training details are given in Appendix C, and §4.5 shows that fine-tuning makes the decisions more accurate.

3.4. Reusing Answers Across Questions

Because a self-contained sub-question names everything it asks about, it has the same meaning, and the same answer, whichever original question it was written for. For example, “In which city is the headquarters of Sazerac Company located?” has the answer “New Orleans” whether it arises from a question about Barton Premium Blend or about Blanton’s, two whiskey brands made by that company. So a QA pair found while answering one question can be used again by any later question that needs it. DeFT-RAG keeps the QA pairs of all questions in a QA cache ℳ\mathcal{M} and checks it before retrieving passages for a new sub-question. It first looks for a stored sub-question with the same wording, ignoring letter case and punctuation. If none is found, it takes the few stored sub-questions most similar to the new one and uses the DM to decide whether any of them has the same meaning, with a strict τ=0.8\tau=0.8, because a wrongly reused answer carries an error into another question. If one does, its answer is reused, without retrieval or an LLM call. Otherwise, the sub-question is answered as usual and the new QA pair is added to ℳ\mathcal{M}. In Figure 2, the first sub-question was answered for an earlier question, so its answer comes from the QA cache (marked “cached”).

3.5. Query Answering Process

Algorithm 1 and Figure 2 show how the components work together to answer a question QQ. DeFT-RAG first retrieves ww passages for QQ, and the DM decides whether they already contain all the evidence needed; if so, LLMans\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{ans}} answers QQ directly from the selected passages (lines 1–3). Otherwise, DeFT-RAG starts with an empty QA table and proceeds one step at a time: LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} writes the next self-contained sub-question, the DM selects the relevant passages retrieved for it, LLMans\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{ans}} answers it, and the pair is added to the QA table (lines 5–9). After each step, the DM checks whether the QA pairs are enough to answer QQ; if so, LLMfin\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{fin}} answers QQ from the QA table (lines 10–11). If this does not happen within TT steps, DeFT-RAG falls back to answering QQ directly from the relevant passages among the top 2​w2w retrieved for it (lines 14–15).

The direct-answer decision lets questions that need only one retrieval be answered in one step, which saves LLM calls; for the other questions, the final answer is built from a short list of QA pairs rather than from a long reasoning trace.

4. Evaluation

4.1. Setup

We evaluate on three multi-hop QA benchmarks, MuSiQue (Trivedi et al., 2022), 2WikiMultiHopQA (2Wiki) (Ho et al., 2020) and HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018), using the 1,000-question test set of each and its passage corpus (11,656, 6,119 and 9,811 passages), as released by the authors of LogicRAG (Chen et al., 2026b). We compare against 13 baselines: answering without retrieval (No Retrieval) and vanilla RAG; seven graph-based methods, LightRAG (Guo et al., 2025), PathRAG (Chen et al., 2026a), HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024), HippoRAG 2 (Gutiérrez et al., 2025), MemGraphRAG (Wu et al., 2026), G3RAG (Li et al., 2026) and LinearRAG (Zhuang et al., 2026); and four iterative methods, IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023), Self-Ask (Press et al., 2023), LogicRAG (Chen et al., 2026b) and Hi-Q (Kim et al., 2026). We do not compare with REAP (Zhu et al., 2026), whose planner and fact extractor are LLMs fine-tuned on trajectories from HotpotQA and 2Wiki, which does not fit our setting of one shared backbone for all systems. All systems share the same backbone LLM, the same embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-4B), temperature 0 and the same output limit; each baseline otherwise keeps its own published settings, such as chunk size.

We use two backbones: gpt-4o-mini, through its API, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, run locally. All baselines retrieve the top k=5k=5 passages per retrieval. DeFT-RAG retrieves the top w=2​k=10w=2k=10 passages, from which the DM keeps the relevant ones. For a fair comparison, it keeps at most five relevant passages at each step (2.1 to 2.4 on average), the same number as the baselines’ top-5. DeFT-RAG takes at most T=6T=6 steps, and all main results are obtained without reuse (§3.4). We report exact match (EM), token F1 and LLM-judged accuracy (LLM-Acc), our main metric, graded with the SimpleQA prompt (Wei et al., 2024). To avoid a model grading its own answers, gpt-4o-mini runs are judged by Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.6 runs by gpt-4o-mini. Differences are tested with the exact McNemar test on paired answers. Appendix E reports the overhead of every method: index building, answering latency, LLM calls and tokens.

4.2. Fine-Tuning the Decision Model

The DM starts from the StartLux-Decision-4B weights (StartLux Labs, 2026) (Qwen3.5 architecture, 4B parameters), which were trained to answer yes/no and multiple-choice questions with probabilities that reflect how often the answer is right. We fine-tune it on data built only from the training splits of the three benchmarks. To make the training inputs look like the test inputs, we split the training questions into groups of 1,000, and each group retrieves from a corpus made of its own passages, just as each test set retrieves from its own corpus. The labels come from the benchmarks’ gold annotations: a passage is relevant if it is a gold supporting passage; a question can be answered directly if all its supporting passages are retrieved; and the QA pairs found so far are enough once they include the answer to every step of the question’s gold decomposition (MuSiQue) or gold evidence (2Wiki). No test question or test-corpus passage appears in the training data, which has 48,036 training and 7,806 development examples (the latter from 15% of the training questions, held out from training). We fine-tune with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, on all linear layers; 32.5M of 4.24B parameters trained), at a learning rate of 10−410^{-4} with 5% warm-up and cosine decay, for one epoch (2,262 steps, about 6.4 hours on two NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPUs). We then adjust the output probabilities with a single temperature parameter fitted on the development examples, never on test questions. Appendix C gives the full data recipe.

4.3. Main Results

Table 2 reports EM, F1 and accuracy on all three benchmarks with both backbones. DeFT-RAG achieves the highest score on all three metrics in all six settings; we discuss accuracy, our main metric, below. Its gains over the second-best system are largest on MuSiQue, which has the longest evidence chains: +5.2+5.2 points over Hi-Q with gpt-4o-mini (0.629 vs. 0.577) and +5.3+5.3 with Qwen3.6 (0.636 vs. 0.583), both significant. On 2Wiki, DeFT-RAG is 2.9 points ahead of LogicRAG with Qwen3.6 (significant) and on par with Self-Ask with gpt-4o-mini (0.852 vs. 0.849). On HotpotQA, it is 3.4 points ahead of Hi-Q with gpt-4o-mini (significant) and on par with Hi-Q and LinearRAG with Qwen3.6 (0.871 vs. 0.864 and 0.857). Against every other baseline, the difference is significant in every setting.

Graph-based methods vary widely: with gpt-4o-mini, LightRAG, PathRAG and HippoRAG fall below vanilla RAG, and even the strongest of them trail DeFT-RAG by at least 10 points on MuSiQue with either backbone, which matches their low full-chain coverage (§2.3). The strongest baselines are iterative methods, but the best of them changes with the benchmark and the backbone: Hi-Q on MuSiQue and HotpotQA, and Self-Ask or LogicRAG on 2Wiki. DeFT-RAG is the only system that is first or on par with the first everywhere.

4.4. Why DeFT-RAG Gives Better Answers

More of the evidence chain, in fewer words.

Table 3 measures, for each MuSiQue question, whether the LLM received all passages needed to answer it, as annotated in the dataset, and how many words of passages it received. DeFT-RAG gives the LLM the full chain for 46% of 3-hop and 18% of 4-hop questions, the highest 3-hop coverage of all systems, with 390 words per question, the fewest of any system and less than half of vanilla RAG’s 870. The systems that cover more chains on some hop count use far more words: Self-Ask covers more 2-hop chains (83%) with 2,590 words, and LinearRAG covers 19% of 4-hop chains with 4,110 words, about ten times as many as DeFT-RAG. These extra words bury the needed passages among many that are not needed, which lowers accuracy (§2.4, Table 1), and they add to the LLM’s input cost. Asking one self-contained sub-question at a time and keeping only the passages the DM judges relevant gives the LLM a short context that still contains the needed evidence.

Effect of passage selection.

To isolate the effect of selection, we turn it off and give the LLM the top-5 retrieved passages, as the baselines do, keeping everything else the same (Table 4). Without selection, accuracy drops on all three benchmarks, by 2.3, 3.7 and 5.3 points on MuSiQue, 2Wiki and HotpotQA; the drop on HotpotQA is significant (p=0.002p=0.002). On 2Wiki and HotpotQA, most of the loss comes from questions answered directly, where the LLM must find the evidence for the whole question in one list of passages. This agrees with Table 1: on questions that can be answered in one retrieval step, a longer list of passages alone barely helps, but keeping only the needed passages from it raises accuracy substantially.

4.5. Effect of Fine-Tuning the Decision Model

Table 5 compares the decisions of the base DM (StartLux-Decision-4B before fine-tuning) and the fine-tuned DM against gold labels. Fine-tuning improves the direct-answer decision the most, for example from 0.850 to 0.933 on MuSiQue, and also improves relevance, most clearly on MuSiQue (0.931 to 0.979), while the enough-facts decision changes little. End to end, on the first 300 MuSiQue questions with gpt-4o-mini, the fine-tuned DM raises accuracy from 0.587 to 0.623.

4.6. Reusing Answers

We run DeFT-RAG with reuse (§3.4) on all 1,000 MuSiQue questions with gpt-4o-mini, answering them in order with one QA cache. Of all sub-questions generated over the 1,000 questions, 23.1% are answered from the cache, which reduces the number of LLM calls by 12.9%. Accuracy does not drop (0.642 with reuse vs. 0.629 without, p=0.18p=0.18), so answers found for earlier questions can be safely reused for later ones.

5. Related Work

Graph-based RAG.

Graph-based methods build a graph over the corpus offline and retrieve along it at answering time. GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) and LightRAG (Guo et al., 2025) extract entities and relations with an LLM and retrieve community summaries or entities, PathRAG (Chen et al., 2026a) retrieves relational paths, HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., 2024) and HippoRAG 2 (Gutiérrez et al., 2025) rank passages with Personalized PageRank from the question’s entities, MemGraphRAG (Wu et al., 2026) builds a layered graph of schemas, facts and passages, and LinearRAG (Zhuang et al., 2026) and G3RAG (Li et al., 2026) build their graphs without LLM extraction. All of these methods retrieve once per question, starting from what the question names, which rarely recovers the full evidence chain beyond two hops (§2.3). DeFT-RAG instead finds the bridge entities at answering time, one self-contained sub-question at a time, and retrieves the full chain for more questions with three or more hops than any of these methods (Table 3).

Iterative RAG.

IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023) uses each new chain-of-thought sentence as the next query, and Self-Ask (Press et al., 2023) poses follow-up questions within a single growing prompt. LogicRAG (Chen et al., 2026b) and REAP (Zhu et al., 2026) plan the sub-questions with their dependencies in advance, and Hi-Q (Kim et al., 2026) and REAP rewrite dependent sub-questions as answers arrive. In these methods, the LLM itself takes on several tasks, often within the same call: planning or writing the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them, keeping track of what is known, and deciding when to stop. DeFT-RAG instead lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time: generating one self-contained sub-question for the next missing piece of information, which removes planning, dependencies and rewriting, and avoids their associated errors; tracking is handled by the QA table, and the yes/no decisions by the fine-tuned DM. Its LLM input stays short, 1,569 tokens per question against 6,140 for Self-Ask (Appendix E), and it achieves the highest accuracy of these methods in every setting (Table 2).

Models for retrieval decisions.

Rerankers (Nogueira et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2023) re-score retrieved passages but still keep a fixed number, and Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al., 2024) uses a trained classifier to choose between no, single and iterative retrieval; Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024), Search-R1 (Jin et al., 2025), R1-Searcher (Song et al., 2025) and Search-o1 (Li et al., 2025) instead train the backbone LLM, or use a reasoning model, to make such decisions. DeFT-RAG uses one fine-tuned DM for the yes/no decisions at every step while the backbone stays unchanged, so any LLM can serve as the backbone, and fine-tuning the DM is much cheaper than training the backbone LLM.

6. Conclusion

We presented DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework for multi-hop question answering built on three components: incremental decomposition into self-contained sub-questions, which avoids planning, dependency and rewriting errors; fine-grained tasks handled outside the LLM, namely rule-based updates to a QA table and yes/no decisions by a fine-tuned lightweight DM; and a QA cache that reuses answers across questions. Across three benchmarks and two backbones, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines, with its largest gains on MuSiQue, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method; reusing answers reduces LLM calls without lowering accuracy.

Appendix A Implementation Details

Table 6 lists the settings used for all results. Beyond Algorithm 1, the implementation retries once on an empty or repeated reply, with a changed input, and uses the following rules.

Additional rules.

A question is answered directly only when the DM judges its passages sufficient (τ=0.7\tau=0.7) and it does not ask for a composite family relation such as a grandparent or an in-law, which is detected by keywords. All results use the same rules on every benchmark and backbone.

How the thresholds were chosen.

The thresholds of 0.5 are the natural cut-off for yes/no probabilities that reflect how often yes is right, and were not tuned. The direct-answer threshold of 0.7 was chosen during development on stored answers of part of the test questions (2Wiki and the first 300 MuSiQue questions), and then kept fixed for all benchmarks and both backbones. The result depends little on this choice: moving the threshold to 0.6 or 0.8 changes the path of at most 13 of the 1,000 questions per benchmark and accuracy by at most 0.1 points on every benchmark (gpt-4o-mini). The reuse threshold of 0.8 was set strict by hand, because a wrongly reused answer carries an error into another question.

{facts}

Question: {question}
Answer:

Decision: relevance of passage ii.

Is `p_i` needed to answer `question`: does it state part of the answer, or a linking fact the reasoning must pass through (e.g., identifying an entity the question refers to only by description)?
Yes: `p_i` states part of the answer, or a linking fact needed to reach it.
No: `p_i` is not needed to answer `question`: it is unrelated or only loosely related.

Decision: direct answer.

Do the passages `p1` through `p10` together contain all the facts needed to answer `question` -- whether stated outright or derivable by combining facts across them?
Yes: Every fact needed is present across the passages; the answer is stated or derivable by connecting them.
No: At least one fact needed to answer is missing and would have to be found elsewhere.

Decision: enough facts.

Has `question` already been answered by the facts in `facts`: does every entity or value the question asks for, or depends on, appear among the facts' answers?
Yes: The facts already give the answer: each step the question depends on is answered in `facts`.
No: Some step the question depends on has not been answered yet, so `question` cannot be answered from `facts` alone.

Decision: same meaning (reuse).

Are `query` and `c_i` the same question: asking for the same piece of information about the same explicitly named entity, so that one correct answer is correct for both?
Yes: Both name the same entity explicitly and ask for the same information; only the wording differs.
No: They differ in entity, property, time, place or scope -- OR either one refers to something without naming it (such as "the tournament" or "the author"), so it is unclear whether they mean the same thing.

Appendix C Decision Model Fine-Tuning Details

Training questions and corpora.

For each benchmark, we sample 3,000 questions from its training split, following the mix of hop counts or question types of the test set, and split them into groups of 1,000. Each group’s corpus consists of the passages of its own questions (MuSiQue about 13,000, 2Wiki about 5,200, HotpotQA about 9,600 passages per group, close to the test corpora of 11,656, 6,119 and 9,811). Every training request retrieves its top 10 passages from its group’s corpus with the embedder and query instruction of DeFT-RAG.

Labels.

All labels come from the training splits’ gold annotations. Relevance: a passage is relevant if it is a gold supporting passage; each request labels all gold passages and three randomly chosen other passages, while all ten passages stay in the request. Direct answer: yes if all gold supporting passages are among the top 10. Enough facts: built from the gold decompositions (MuSiQue) and gold evidence (2Wiki): the answers to only the first steps give “no”, the answers to all steps give “yes”, a wrong answer to a step gives “no”, and the answers to all steps plus an unrelated QA pair give “yes”. We add enough-facts items taken from runs of DeFT-RAG on training questions, labelled by the same rule, and items whose QA pairs use self-contained sub-questions, as DeFT-RAG writes them. The same-meaning decision is not fine-tuned.

Leakage checks.

All 1,000 test questions of each benchmark come from its official validation split; none of them is in the training data, and no training question text is identical to a test question. Training questions whose gold passage appears in any test corpus are skipped, so that no test-corpus passage is ever shown in training.

Training and probability adjustment.

The final data has 48,036 training and 7,806 development examples. LoRA settings are given in §4.2; training used micro-batches of 8,192 tokens, gradient accumulation to an effective batch equal to the base model’s single-GPU default, gradient checkpointing and gradient clipping at 1.0. A single temperature for yes/no probabilities is fitted on the development examples (1.08).

Appendix D Experimental Details for Baselines

All systems use the same backbone, the same embedding model (Qwen3-Embedding-4B, last-token pooling, with the query instruction applied to queries only), temperature 0, top-​p=1\text{top-}p=1 and the same output limit of 3,072 tokens; the reasoning mode of Qwen3.6 is turned off for every system. Each baseline keeps the settings of its released code or paper that define the method, such as chunk size and graph construction, and all baselines retrieve the top k=5k=5 passages per retrieval (§4.1). Systems that build the same kind of index share it: HippoRAG and MemGraphRAG reuse the index built by HippoRAG 2 (for MemGraphRAG, only the passage embeddings, after we checked that the passage sets are identical), and PathRAG reuses LightRAG’s graph. Every system’s answers are graded by the same script with the same judge prompt, and missing answers count as wrong.

Appendix E Overhead Analysis

Table 7 reports, for every method with gpt-4o-mini, the cost of building the index and the cost of answering each question. Its last row replaces the local DM of DeFT-RAG with Jev, a closed decision model accessed through an API.

Index.

DeFT-RAG, vanilla RAG and the iterative methods only embed the passages, which takes about five minutes per corpus and no LLM calls. The graph-based methods that extract a graph with the LLM need from about 2,100 (LightRAG) to 147,000 (MemGraphRAG) LLM calls and 11 to 114 million tokens per corpus, and up to 18 hours of build time; this cost is paid again when the corpus changes.

Answering.

DeFT-RAG gives the LLM fewer input tokens per question than every other iterative method (1,569, against 1,926 to 13,928), and it produces the fewest output tokens of all methods (33), because each task asks for a short output; it also makes fewer LLM calls than Self-Ask and Hi-Q (4.8, against 6.3 and 6.6). Its latency is the highest (median 9.9 s).

Where the latency comes from.

Most of the answering time of DeFT-RAG goes to its frequent calls to the local DM, which selects the relevant passages at every step and makes the other decisions. Per question, DeFT-RAG makes 7.0, 6.3 and 3.2 DM calls on MuSiQue, 2Wiki and HotpotQA, at 1.6 to 1.8 s each, as the DM runs on one GPU, one request at a time, over inputs of up to ten passages. These calls take 12.5 of the 20.4 s mean answering time on MuSiQue, 10.3 of 16.7 s on 2Wiki and 5.2 of 7.8 s on HotpotQA, about 60 to 70%. With Jev in place of the DM, at about 0.16 s per call, the median latency falls from 9.9 to 5.0 s, and the mean answering time to 8.2, 7.7 and 3.6 s on the three benchmarks, while accuracy stays within 1.2 points of the DM’s (0.618, 0.857 and 0.867, against 0.629, 0.852 and 0.874). Most of the added latency thus comes from how the DM is served, not from the method itself.

Appendix F Case Studies

All cases are taken from the runs in Table 2 (gpt-4o-mini backbone); each line shows a sub-question and the answer DeFT-RAG found for it.

Where it works: a three-hop chain.

“When did the city where the headquarters of Barton Premium Blend’s manufacturer is located elect its first black mayor?” (gold: 1970s). DeFT-RAG asks one self-contained sub-question at a time:

What is the name of the manufacturer of Barton Premium Blend? →\rightarrow Sazerac Company
In which city is the headquarters of Sazerac Company located? →\rightarrow New Orleans
When did New Orleans elect its first black mayor? →\rightarrow 1970s

After the third QA pair, the DM judges the QA pairs enough and LLMfin\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{fin}} answers “1970s”. Self-Ask’s first follow-up skips the manufacturer (“What city is the headquarters of Barton Premium Blend’s manufacturer located in?”), takes Bardstown, Kentucky as the answer, and finally answers “Information not available”; Hi-Q also gives no answer, and LogicRAG answers “No”.

Where it works, but not in order.

For “Who sent naval ships to the body of water that joins the Atlantic and the sea where the Rhine ends?” (gold: Caesar), the question behind the example in §3.1, the DM first judges the retrieved passages insufficient (0.15), and DeFT-RAG asks:

Who sent naval ships to the body of water that joins the Atlantic? →\rightarrow Caesar
What is the name of the sea where the Rhine ends? →\rightarrow North Sea
What is the name of the body of water that joins the Atlantic and the North Sea? →\rightarrow English Channel

The first sub-question skips ahead to the last hop with a vague description and happens to retrieve the right answer. The DM does not stop there (enough facts: 0.44), but only after the chain through the North Sea and the English Channel is complete (0.70); the final answer is “Caesar”.

Where it fails: nested sub-questions.

Bridge-comparison questions in 2Wiki compare two films through their directors. “Which film has the director who is older than the other, Airheads or Return To Cabin By The Lake?” (gold: Return To Cabin By The Lake):

Who is the director of Airheads? →\rightarrow Michael Lehmann
What is the date of birth of Michael Lehmann? →\rightarrow March 30, 1957
What is the date of birth of the director of Return To Cabin By The Lake? →\rightarrow (no answer)
What is the name of the director of Return To Cabin By The Lake? →\rightarrow Po-Chih Leong
What is the date of birth of Po-Chih Leong? →\rightarrow 31 December 1939
What film did Po-Chih Leong direct? →\rightarrow (no answer)

The third sub-question is not self-contained: it asks for the birth date of a director who has not been named yet, and retrieval finds no answer. DeFT-RAG recovers in the next two steps, but the DM does not judge the four QA pairs enough, the loop reaches its step limit, and the fallback answers “Airheads”. On 2Wiki bridge-comparison questions, 38% of such nested sub-questions get no answer, against 4% of sub-questions that ask for a single relation, and 75 of 235 of these questions reach the step limit or repeat themselves; this is the main reason DeFT-RAG only matches Self-Ask on 2Wiki with gpt-4o-mini (Table 2).

Where it fails: the right entity, the wrong fact.

“When was the person who Messi’s goals in Copa del Rey compared to get signed by Barcelona?” (gold: June 1982). DeFT-RAG first finds the right person (“Diego Maradona”), so it does not shift back to Messi; but it then asks for Maradona’s date of birth instead of the date he was signed, the DM accepts these QA pairs as enough, and the final answer (“30 October 1984”) is wrong. The rule that tells LLMsub\mathrm{LLM}_{\mathrm{sub}} to ask for dates of birth when comparing ages (Appendix B) may have pulled the sub-question towards a birth date.

Remaining errors.

On 2Wiki with gpt-4o-mini, an analysis of the 148 wrong answers attributed only about 19 to the DM’s decisions; most of the others come from the backbone, such as nested sub-questions or wrong readings of correct passages.
